strengths: Rigorous theoretical formulation: The paper provides a thorough mathematical proof showing that causal decoder-only Transformers are real-analytic functions and that the parameter collision set for any two distinct discrete prompts has Lebesgue measure zero.

Preservation under training: Unlike previous work that only studied random initializations, this paper rigorously establishes that finite steps of gradient descent (and mini-batch SGD) preserve absolute continuity of parameter distributions, guaranteeing that injectivity persists throughout training.

Extensive empirical verification: The authors conduct large-scale empirical experiments across multiple open-weight LLM families (GPT-2, Gemma-3 up to 12B, Llama-3.1, Mistral, Phi-4) and billions of pairwise comparisons, demonstrating that minimum pairwise distances remain well above numerical collision thresholds.

Constructive inversion algorithm: SIPIT operationalizes the causal structure of Transformers to achieve exact input reconstruction in $O(T |\mathcal{V}|)$ worst-case time, accelerated practically via gradient-guided search in the embedding space.
weaknesses: Disconnect between theoretical focus and algorithmic requirement: The theoretical analysis heavily emphasizes the last-token representation $r(s; \theta) \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and contrasts itself against prior work (such as Sutter et al., 2025) that relies on the full sequence of hidden states. However, SIPIT explicitly requires access to the entire sequence of hidden states $\hat{H}^{(\ell)} \in \mathbb{R}^{T \times d}$ across all positions $t=1,\dots,T$. Inverting from the full sequence of causal states position-by-position is conceptually much simpler (since position $t$ only depends on prefix $\pi$ and candidate $s_t$), and the paper should clarify this distinction more prominently in the introduction and abstract.

Finite-precision vs. real-analyticity: The mathematical results rely fundamentally on infinite-precision real arithmetic ($\mathbb{R}^p$ with Lebesgue measure). In practical deployments, LLMs operate under finite precision (FP16, BF16, or FP8). While the empirical section shows margins above $10^{-3}$, a formal discussion on minimum margin scaling with sequence length and floating-point discretization is missing.

Scope of the inversion evaluation: The empirical evaluation of SIPIT in Section 4.2 is restricted to GPT-2 Small with relatively short sequences (20 tokens in Table 2, up to 200 tokens in Figure 6). Demonstrating SIPIT on modern architectures with large vocabularies (e.g., Gemma-3 with $|\mathcal{V}| > 256\text{k}$) would significantly strengthen the empirical claims regarding runtime feasibility.

Baselines for prompt inversion: Comparing SIPIT against HardPrompts is somewhat unaligned, as HardPrompts was designed for approximate prompt discovery via CLIP similarity rather than white-box hidden state inversion. Comparing against dedicated feature inversion / embedding inversion baselines or standard greedy next-token matching would be more insightful.

strengths: Clear, rigorous mathematical formulation establishing that standard Transformer architectures with real-analytic activations (such as GELU or tanh) and layer normalization define real-analytic maps with respect to their parameters.
Well-structured proof demonstrating that parameter updates under gradient descent (and mini-batch SGD) preserve absolute continuity of parameter distributions with respect to the Lebesgue measure.

Extensive empirical sanity checks over billions of prompt pairs across multiple open-source LLM families (GPT-2, Gemma-3, Llama-3.1, Mistral, Phi-4) showing that pairwise L2 distances between hidden states remain strictly bounded away from zero in the tested subsets.
weaknesses: Severe conceptual disconnect between the theoretical claims and the proposed inversion algorithm (SIPIT): The paper repeatedly emphasizes as its central theoretical insight that the *last-token representation* alone is almost-surely injective and identifies the full prompt (e.g., in the Abstract, Section 1, Section 2 note 2, and Section 5). However, SIPIT (Algorithm 1) does *not* invert the last-token representation. Instead, it requires the entire sequence of hidden states across all token positions (H in R^{T x d}). If one only possesses the last-token state, SIPIT cannot operate.

Triviality of the algorithmic setting: Given the entire sequence of layer-l hidden states h_1, ..., h_T and causal masking, recovering each token s_t given the prefix s_{1:t-1} reduces to an exhaustive or gradient-guided search over a single discrete token from the finite vocabulary V (typically 32k to 128k items). Finding which of the |V| candidates matches the observed h_t is computationally straightforward and does not substantiate the claim of having solved the hard problem of inverting Transformer representations.

The theoretical result relies heavily on the finiteness of the input domain combined with infinite-precision real numbers: Because the context length K and vocabulary V are bounded, the prompt set V^{<=K} is finite. For any real-analytic architecture, the set of parameters causing any two fixed prompts to collide is either R^p or a set of Lebesgue measure zero. Ruling out the identically zero case via a single manual construction is standard, and taking a finite union of null sets trivially preserves measure zero. However, in actual digital hardware operating under finite precision (bfloat16 or float32), the continuous measure-zero argument breaks down: by the Pigeonhole Principle, mapping sequences of moderate length (where |V|^K >> 2^{16d}) to a finite set of machine-representable floats must inevitably produce collisions.

Narrow experimental evaluation of SIPIT: The inversion experiments are limited to 100 prompts of length 20 on GPT-2 Small. The baselines are poorly matched: HardPrompts is designed for optimizing prompts towards text/image targets rather than step-by-step state matching from full hidden activations, making its 0% accuracy an uninformative baseline.

Misleading framing regarding privacy and invertibility: The paper claims that 'user inputs remain fully recoverable' and 'there is no free privacy once data enters a Transformer', but this holds in practice only if an attacker already captures the continuous activation vector at every intermediate sequence position, which is unrealistic in typical black-box or API deployment scenarios.

strengths: Rigorous mathematical formulation: The paper takes a formal, real-analytic perspective on decoder-only Transformers, thoroughly proving joint real-analyticity of common architectural blocks (multi-head attention, LayerNorm with epsilon > 0, analytic activations like GELU/tanh) and establishing that parameter collision sets have Lebesgue measure zero.

Sound proof of absolute continuity preservation: Showing that finite-horizon gradient descent updates preserve the absolute continuity of the parameter distribution via local invertibility and the non-vanishing Jacobian determinant at an explicit witness point is well-constructed.

Extensive empirical verification of separability: The authors perform large-scale empirical testing (billions of pairwise comparisons across GPT-2, Gemma-3, LLaMA-3.1, Mistral, Phi-4, and TinyStories) confirming that hidden representations are well-separated in practice.
Clear writing and complete appendix: The paper is well-written, clearly organized, and provides detailed step-by-step proofs and dimension bookkeeping in the supplementary material.
weaknesses: Fundamental mismatch between theoretical focus and algorithmic operationalization: The paper heavily emphasizes as its primary distinction from prior work (e.g., Sutter et al., 2025) that it establishes injectivity for the last-token representation r(s; theta), which it calls 'our quantity of operational interest' (Remark 13). However, the inversion algorithm SIPIT does not invert from the last-token representation; it requires the entire sequence of hidden state vectors H^{(l)} in R^{T x d} across all token positions t = 1, ..., T. Inverting token-by-token given every intermediate hidden state vector h_t is drastically easier than inverting from the last-token representation alone, creating a disconnect between the paper's central theoretical claim and its practical algorithm.

Significance of almost-sure injectivity on finite discrete domains: Because the input space V^{<=K} is finite while the representation space R^d is continuous, any non-degenerate real-analytic function almost surely separates all inputs. Practically, when researchers discuss Transformers being 'lossy' or 'collapsing representations', they refer to finite-precision limits (FP16/BF16/INT8), ill-conditioning, or representation bottlenecks when compressing long sequences into fixed-width vectors. Establishing measure-zero collisions under infinite-precision real analysis does not address these practical senses of information loss.

Unrealistic threat model and limited baseline comparison for SIPIT: SIPIT assumes complete white-box access to the model and unquantized access to all intermediate hidden states h_1, ..., h_T. Under this strong threat model, exact causal reconstruction is expected. The paper dismisses prior inversion work (e.g., Morris et al., Nazir et al.) as approximate, but those methods tackle significantly harder and more practical black-box or logprob/logit-only settings.

Narrow experimental evaluation of inversion: SIPIT is evaluated on only 100 prompts of length 20 using only a single small model (GPT-2 Small). There is no inversion evaluation on larger modern architectures (such as LLaMA-3.1 or Gemma-3), nor any evaluation under realistic inference environments with FP16/BF16 precision, noisy activations, or longer sequence lengths.
